A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work, with matching core methods, theorems and original experiments. Text, equations, figures and appendices support a reliable comparison; the expanded material in v2 is identifiable.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic-data and CIFAR-10 reconstruction experiments with random features, two-layer networks and ResNets in Section 5 and Appendix E.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original classification, Tiny-ImageNet, transformer and robustness results in Section 5 and Appendix E.3.

M1.justification: The projection loss in Eq. (11) and its optimization remain unchanged. Appendix E.3 adds a limited procedural suggestion for unknown dataset size: increase the number of reconstructed candidates until duplicates appear to estimate n. This is proposed as a practical heuristic, rather than an established new algorithm.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained spherical-data and CIFAR-10 experiments, v2 adds higher-resolution Tiny-ImageNet reconstruction, synthetic classification with sign-generated labels, and reconstruction without the exact training-set size. These broaden both the represented data and the information requirements of the reconstruction task.

E2.justification: Neither version evaluates competing reconstruction algorithms against the proposed method. Optimal Brain Surgeon is newly used to produce pruned target models in v2, not as a competing reconstruction method.

E3.justification: v2 adds classification training with logistic/cross-entropy losses, full-batch gradient descent at step size 0.001 for one million steps, transformer embedding-size sweeps, and regularization/pruning settings. Appendix E.3 also introduces candidate-count variations and a learning-rate experiment capped at 60,000 reconstruction iterations. These are additional protocols; the original experiments' settings are retained.

E4.justification: New Appendix E.3 tests sensitivity to reconstruction learning rate, incorrect candidate-set size, ridge regularization and pruning (Figures 11–12 and 15–16). These directly examine optimization failures and reconstruction robustness beyond v1's retained span-inclusion and activation-sign analyses.

E5.justification: Appendix D newly explains that seeds independently initialize network parameters and reconstruction variables. Existing four-seed and ten-seed results retain their run counts and mean/standard-deviation reporting. The additional ten-seed experiments do not establish increased replication of earlier results.

E6.justification: The original plotted results and reconstruction images are retained. New results cover classification, Tiny-ImageNet and transformers, plus findings that excessive learning rates prevent convergence, underestimated dataset size produces mixed images, excess candidates produce duplicates, fixed ridge penalties preserve similar thresholds, and pruning increases reconstruction difficulty.

T1.justification: The assumptions, main theorems and proofs in Appendices A–C are unchanged. Appendix E.3 adds the ridge objective, its closed-form solution and a spectral scaling argument explaining why fixed regularization becomes negligible as p grows (Eqs. 168–170). The expanded main proof sketch restates reasoning already present in v1's appendix.

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory contributions and central conclusion retain the same reconstruction-threshold claim, theoretical scope and projection-based reconstruction proposal. The expanded experiments support these claims without redefining the main contributions.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly separates fitting the parameter vector from satisfying the full feature-span hypothesis, explains the obstacle to extending Theorem 2 beyond n = 2, and clarifies that whole-dataset reconstruction limits do not prevent individual-sample memorization. Appendix E.3 additionally interprets failures and applicability under size uncertainty, learning-rate variation, regularization and pruning.

D1.justification: Documentation adds classification training settings, Tiny-ImageNet class selection and preprocessing, its reconstruction step size of 8000, and ablation ranges and budgets. Transformer and pruning configurations are also described. The core optimizer implementation, hardware disclosure and code-access information remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for vision transformers, Tiny-ImageNet, Optimal Brain Surgeon and Vardi–Yehudai–Shamir's memorization result. Section 2 adds a brief discussion of sublinear-parameter label memorization under separability. The broader positioning against prior reconstruction work is retained.

P1.justification: v2 expands the theory-to-algorithm explanation, adds Remark 2 and experimental paragraphs, broadens the natural-image heading, and introduces Appendix E.3. Most existing prose and the main section order remain intact, so this is an extension with localized rewriting.

P2.justification: v2 adds substantial new plots and image montages for classification, Tiny-ImageNet, transformers and robustness studies (Figures 5, 8 and 11–17). Original Figures 5–8 survive as Figures 6, 7, 9 and 10. The Tiny-ImageNet images are redisplayed in Figures 5 and 14; this is not two independent results.

improvement.justification: v1's empirical support concentrated on square-loss models and left important practical dependencies untested. v2 substantially strengthens that support through classification experiments and controlled tests of optimization, dataset-size knowledge, regularization and pruning, while explaining relevant failure conditions and theoretical limits. Small evaluation subsets and the unresolved general-n and optimization guarantees remain, but the broader evidence materially improves the paper.
